utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you're to continue with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Karavelic. Let us continue what we started yesterday. In order not to come back to this issue later, let me ask you this. If your superior commander or the Chief of the General Staff would give you an order and you failed to carry out that order, what kind of consequences would you suffer as a result?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At any rate, negative consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please show the witness P498.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That was the first document presented to you by my learned colleague the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's P498. Document P498 is an order dated the 7th of November, 1994. Please, it's not a map. Can my learned friend, the Prosecutor, help me? It's an order dated the 7th of November; an order issued by Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, is that the ter number 02777? Because I think the order that my friend is looking for bears the ter number 02106.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. 65 ter 02777 is P498, which is what we have up on screen right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think my learned friend might be looking for P496 then, 02106.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, with regard to this document, you personally know nothing. You have no knowledge except what you can see here that it was drafted by General Mladic's office. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about the document per se, but I know about the activity and how it took place.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness's second microphone be turned on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at this order and under items 1, 2, and 3, each one of them stipulates that certain things are explicitly forbidden. So if such an order is being issued, is then a subordinate officer allowed to act in contravention of that order; in this instances, the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order has a very specific significance .

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's not what I was asking you. That was not my question. Please answer my question which reads: If there is an explicit thing forbidding something three times in an order, can then a subordinate officer fail to comply? Is he allowed to do that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me just to briefly clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I kindly ask for my question to be given an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me hear your answer, and I will determine whether you have answered the question. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes and no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, yes in what respect; and no in what respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in the sense that my answer was no, if you look at item 3, which reads: "I forbid all use of weapons of bigger calibre on civilian targets in Sarajevo without my approval," which means, in other words, that this order was issued on specific circumstances. And, therefore, General Ratko Mladic or the superior officer who issued this order puts a kind of restriction on this activity not to be pursued at this moment due to specific political consequences that might arise, and that in the previous period this was a practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a very simplified explanation, and I don't think the witness should be allowed to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You know nothing about this, but now you have ventured upon a kind of analysis that does not stem from any direct knowledge that you might have.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking on the basis of what I'm reading here, and I issued identical orders to those of General Milosevic. We went to the same school, and we had the same education and training. I'm only construing what I can read here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the event that you gave an order to someone, can your subordinate abuse his position and fail to comply?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issue here is what the he is ordered to do. If it is something in contravention of the Geneva Conventions or against the state, then he must not carry out this order, irrespective of whoever issued it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Not you yourself, but your subordinate?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Makes no difference. It applies to the entire chain of command, irrespective of what level we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us continue where we left off yesterday. In response to His Honour Judge Robinson's question about Light Infantry Brigade, I would like to you to tell me whether within the 1st Corps of the BH army there was engineer unit, military police, artillery? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that existed in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps in terms of structure existed in my corps as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was there a light artillery division of anti-aircraft Defence?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was there an HVO brigade?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was it based in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was the strength of that HVO unit?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a precise number, but I think it was about 2.000 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: After that you also had communications units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You also had under your command and control, special MUP units, Lasta Bosna was the name?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were all police units subordinated to your command?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not a single one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have displayed for the witness DD00-1636. That's Sefer Halilovic's book entitled, "The Cunning Strategy," page 10 in the B/C/S version, page 3 in the English version. There's a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you can see what is written here. A decision on resubordination of units of reserve forces of the Minister of the Interior to the units of the army of the Bosnia and Herzegovina, and item 1 reads: "All reserve unit of the Minister of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina are to be resubordinated to the Main Staff of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina for the purpose of carrying out military actions against the aggressor. 27th of June, 1992," signed by the President of the Presidency about much the army of BH Alija Izetbegovic? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that precisely as a result of this order issued by Sefer Halilovic, he experienced what he later experienced. And I think it is very important for me to give the answer, and it is good for the Chamber to know. He attempted to put the entire MUP under his control, which resulted in a very serious conflict between him and President Izetbegovic; and after that, this disagreement was never resolved between the two, and he never managed to place any police units under his control.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I didn't ask you that. It was published in the book called, "The Cunning Strategy." However, this is an order issued by Alija Izetbegovic personally on the 27th of June. I'm asking you about this order to resubordinate all reserve police units to the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that Mr. Pusina was dismissed from his duties; and as far as I know, there order was never carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you don't know that there was an order in place all the time instructing the police to be permanently under your jurisdiction that is the army leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, since you mentioned Sefer Halilovic, you know that in his book, I presume you have read this book?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read parts of the book not the whole of it, because I don't take to be a serious book.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. His assertion in the book that his wife and his brother were -- and his wife's brother were killed by an explosive planted and activated by remote control, because they were thinking that he would be also there; is that true?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is sick. The people who think that must be sick.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So the second thing is true, that it was a shell fired from the VRS positions.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have this order admitted into evidence. It's been translated and it's a book that was published, and I received this translation from the CLSS as an official translation because the entire book has been translated. And I would like there book to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see Ms. Edgerton on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, of course, I have no objection to the admission of pages from the book of Mr. Halilovic admitted into evidence, and would simply request that the record reflect that these are pages extracted from the book of Sefer Halilovic, rather than a copy of a decision implemented by the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What are the pages to be admitted, Mr. Tapuskovic? I see page 10. Is there another page?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, at this moment page 10, which is the 225th page of that book in B/C/S. Well, I don't know what the page is in English, but it's page 3 in the English version of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This document is already marked for identification, pending translation. So since we now have a translation of -- at any rate, this page, page 10, we will admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D133.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karavelic, now I'm going to show you document DD00-1175, dated the 20th of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have a translation. The document is of the 20th of May, 1995. The Sarajevo division and then underneath it says: "Howitzer 105 millimetres, first smaller artillery" -- it has to do with a howitzer that is being resubordinated to the 102nd Combat Brigade; is that right, is that what is it written in this document? And Fikret Prevljak orders as follows. Prepare a VP, that is correct is to say, a military position for the 105th millimetre howitzer in accordance with the last order. Immediately camouflage the artillery piece in the area of the military sector obvious and protect it against reconnaissance by UN forces. My question is: Lasta is a MUP unit; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in this order it has nothing to do what you have been saying. Lasta is a signal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So it's not the MUP unit called Lasta?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that this order of Prevljak's, the order issued by the commander of the 102nd Division, to camouflage artillery pieces and to hide it primarily from the UN, is that correct? If this was written by your immediate subordinate for the 12th Division?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Properly. Artillery pieces were hidden from everyone except for one's own crew. And why would one have to trust the members of the international force?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were there many weapons in Sarajevo that were hidden from the UN?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were hardly any, if any at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that what it says further on that positions should be prepared for this weapon in order to cover certain axis Krivloci, Blagovac, Medakovic, Trebevic, Lukavica for certain actions, activity. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, probably. If there is a surprise attack that we have weapons that nobody knows of, that we have those weapons there in order to prevent an attack or repel it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could document DD00-1175 which does have a translation, be admitted into evidence as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D142, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That was in May 1995. Here comes another order issued by Prevljak. The document is DD00-0745.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: See? The command of the 12th division on the 8th of May, preparation and engagement of MUP units that is to say in the month and May and paragraph 1 says: "Establish permanent communication with the chiefs of the PS in the zone of responsibility of the brigade and state precisely the place, role and task of MUP units. Again what we have here is a decision clearly stating the tasks of the MUP on the 8th of May, 1995 issued by the commander of the 12th division, Prevljak. I got all these documents from the archives of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is this correct or not?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have to clarify something here. This document only has to do with the local police, police stations in municipalities. This has nothing to do with police units or say special police units at a higher level. So what is this all about? In order to use police forces from time to time for certain combat actions police forces doing nothing otherwise in municipal organs an agreement was reached between the commander of the General Staff and the Minister of Police, that these police forces from local level be used -- could be used by brigade commanders that are there in a specific area. In order to avoid a lengthy procedure of sending requests from the brigade commander to the division commander; then the division commander to the corps commander; and then the corps commander to the General Staff; the General Staff to the Supreme Command Izetbegovic; and then he takes this down to the Minister of the Police; and then down their chain. It's a lengthy process. That is why this order says that at a given point in time, the defence line was in jeopardy at a given point, and he give as green light to the commander or commanders, to be able to use those police forces at a given point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could DDOO-0745 be admitted into evidence, along with the official translation thereof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D143, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to put D61 to the witness now, the one that my colleague, the Prosecutor, already put to the witness yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karavelic, this is an order of the 6th of June -- of July, 1995, and you said yesterday that that was correct. But you said it was all done in accordance with the agreement, as you explained to us yesterday, for defence purposes, right?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My question on the 6th of July, 1995, in the zone of responsibility of the 12th Division, what was under way was an offensive of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina that had started as far back as the 15th of June. So in that stage the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was on the offensive. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 15th of June, we started an offensive from the outer area of the city of Sarajevo with a view to deblocking and opening up the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't finished. This offensive ended towards the end of June, and immediately after that the forces of the SRK started fierce offensive activity from Grbavica towards the Presidency, trying to inflict a deadly blow. I think this has to do precisely with that period, precisely the beginning of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as far as this document is concerned, D61, I don't know whether we've clarified this actually. This was a document that was awaiting translation, so it was mark the for identification as D61. So now it should not be MFI, but it should be a full-fledged Defence exhibit. Oh, yes. It became an exhibit yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It became an exhibit yesterday, Your Honours, and it was an oversight on my part when the Prosecutor was dealing with it. It was admitted because there was a translation there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It was admitted yesterday? I will just ask the court deputy to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It was originally used by the Defence on the 14th of February, and we have marked it for identification at the time as D61; and, yesterday, the 27th of March, it was actually admitted through the Prosecution as D61.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, now I have document DD00-0727. Up until this moment, it was marked as D62, MFI, because there was no translation for it. But now I do have a translation that I got from the CLSS, and now I would like to put it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, put it to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's the document, Mr. Karavelic. The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, command of the 12th Corps, on the 23rd of August 1995, order to carry out active combat operations. Is that right? Is that exactly what it says there?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is not the way it is written there. It's the command of the 12th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. But in that order -- I'm not going to read 1.1, but 1.2 says, under the heading of MUP units, you said it was a code, Lasta. "The Lasta units are to take up positions from the positions of the 104th," and then it say what is the position is. "At the UN checkpoint for Kula where they are to be at the ready to prevent enemy incursions from the direction of Kula." First question: It is stated clearly here that Lasta is a MUP unit? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is absolutely nothing in dispute there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But in the case of the previous document that they were dealing with a few moments ago, you said that Lasta was some kind of a code?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. That's what I'm saying again. Take a look at it and you will see for yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Under 1.3 -- or rather, 1.2, 3. "PTD unit of the Bosna Detachment is to reach the rampart from the airport neighbourhood to the hangar within the airport."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could we please see the previous page again. That is where the relevant text is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you show the previous page again for the benefit of the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And since this is a two-page document, perhaps I could -- I have a hard copy here, and it might assist the witness in answers -- clarifying his question, if he is able to see both pages of the document before answering a question. It's a two-page document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you may pass that to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct what it says here under 1.2, or rather, this other asterik, what I read out?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is what is written in the document. What is there for me to confirm, whether it is correct or not? The document itself says that that is correct. It is not my document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But the document belongs to your subordinate officer. I hope that he could not have issued this kind of an order without your approval?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could have. He could have. Of course, he could have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But in the spirit of your orders and instructions?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the spirit of general yearly plans of activities and action. The division commander is an independent commander with regard to a great many issues, just as I am corps commander in relation to the General Staff, and also brigade commander vis-a-vis the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you are the commander of the 1st Corps of the 12th Division, and the 14th and the 16th, and it is for you to say what your divisions are going to do? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through general plans. It depends on the degree of detail you go into, and what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Only what is stated in the document?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could have carried out these things independently without my knowledge. This is minor activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at the second page now. In the English version, it's the second page, too. You have the document, and at the end, it is the one-but-last instruction in the order, stating that "Lasta according to the plan is going to provide fire support."

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was the number you gave?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The one-but-last paragraph. The one-but-last paragraph of that document, page 2.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one-but-last paragraph. Well, there are numbers aren't there? 1.7, 1.8?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let's not waste any time. It's the one but last?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Fire support according to the Lasta plan." Can you not see that this it a signal? Can you not see that this Lasta has nothing to do with the Lasta unit? It is just a coincidence, so then there is this unit called Lasta, that is indeed referred to, but then there is this plan Lasta, as well. These are two completely different things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Honourable Witness, my point is that this has to do with the what I first read out to you, the MUP units?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is no disputing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document DD00 --

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, look at the end of the second page. It says who this document was submitted to, and see it is not submitted to the command of the 1st Corps. It is not submitted to me, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You want to say that was done without your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, don't you see the document, that it wasn't sent to me? If it had been of importance for me, it would have been sent to me and that was up the commander of the division to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to interpret this?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I'm going to interpret this because you said that I was the responsible person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you're claiming that Prevljak as the commander of the 12th Division and you were the commander of the entire corps --

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Alija Izetbegovic was commander in chief of the entire army. You don't understand the chain of command and the essence of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. It is going to be up to the Chamber to decide, and I kindly ask for this document to be admitted into evidence. It's number DD00-0727 with a translation, and that a number be assigned to it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is was previously marked for identification on the 14th of February as -- as D62, so we will admit it as D62.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have one of the very rare documents that I'm going to show today without the translation; and according to the CLSS, I will get the translation on the 10th of April. The number of the document is DD00-1177. Can we just please show this document to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is the document, Witness. It's dated the 11th of June. It's another order, and it again refers to Bosna. And the instruction is to form a number of units MB 120-millimetres and mortars 82 metres four pieces and the deployment of troops. It has also been signed by Fikret Prevljak. Can you tell me that since this is the document you see and signed by Prevljak is something that has to do with the activity of your units in Sarajevo on the 11th of June?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document shows that he has been assigned a police unit of the MUP Bosna or part of the units in order to carry out a specific task. Since this unit didn't have mortars, it probably requested support, and he complied and established a temporary formation; i.e., a mortar company with a number of mortar and attached it to the last unit and this unit, of course, operated under his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can document DD00-1177 be marked for identification, please, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And under item 3, I'm sorry, if I may, it says that the mortar company will be resubordinated to the Bosna detachment until the execution of the task and thereafter the combatants will be returned to their base units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We mark it for identification. May I ask the court deputy to investigate the temperature in the courtroom. I find it's a bit warm.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be taken care of and this will be marked as D144. Correct, this will be marked for identification as D144.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karavelic, you provided an explanation with regard to MUP activities as part of the activities of the 1st Corps of the ABiH army. Let me ask you directly. In the offensive that began on the 15th of June, did the 3rd and the 7th Corps took part, as well as some other corps?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. My corps, the 3rd and the 7th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand corrected. My corps, the 4th and the 7th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You know that as part of the 3rd and the 7th Corps there was a very important unit called El Mudjahid, made up of several hundred combatants from Arabic countries?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know something about it but not much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show to you a document that I received a long time ago from the Prosecution. The Prosecution have their own translation. It hasn't been translated by the CLSS, but, rather, probably by the Prosecution administration. It's DD00-1672. We have a translation of this document as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karavelic, take a look at this. Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina army of the RbiH 1st Corps command military security service section. It has its reference number, Sarajevo, the 9th of June, 1995. And in this document, in the first paragraph it says as follows: Acting in accordance with the order bearing the above mentioned number, operation Vranduk was introduced to the 1st Corps aiming to discover and eliminate possible intelligence activities and other illegal activities of citizens of African/Asian countries within the force of the RBiH Army 1st Corps. And in paragraph 3, it reads as follows:--

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This is a document of several pages. It's a 4 page document and perhaps the witness could be given a copy of the document before being asked to comment on any portion of it. I'm only raising that, Your Honour, because it's several pages long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, do you have a copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in B/C/S there are only two pages and I can easily show it to the witness. There are only two pages --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 3, it reads as follows: "OSVB of the 115th Mountain Brigade as part of the 12th division through interview with a source, a former member of the 306th Mountain Brigade within the 7th corps which had taken part in combat operations together with El Mudjahid , acquire the following intelligence about this detachment and its members, persons from Asian and African countries. I'm not going to read the whole document to you, and on page 2, this is what the document says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, would you explain to the Chamber the significance of this line of cross-examination and, in particular, how -- how the issues, raised by it, impact on the question of guilt or innocence of the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, I would like to read only one portion of this document that is linked to my question. First of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What I asked to you explain and not to read something else in defiance of what I told to you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Honourable President. I wanted to use this document as a basis for establishing the fact that in the offensive that lasted from the 15th of June, 1995, several hundred members of this unit took part, and it is written here that they operated on the principle that they didn't know what the notion of the "prisoner of war" was. It says here that there were 300 foreigners from Arabic countries taking part in this operation and according to this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the significance of that? What if they did take part in? What if, as you say, 300 foreigners took part in this operation. How does that impact on the guilt or innocence of the accused? That's what we are concerned with here. We are not writing a history of these events. Our concern is far more specific. And if you can't explain to me, I'm not allowing you to ask any more questions along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will have to do my best and explain this to you. The intelligence service of the VRS already had information that once a prisoner in other battlefields falls into the hands of this detachment they were immediately executed. Therefore the fear of loosing positions would result in every captured soldier of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina be executed on the spot because they did not recognise the notion of a POW. That was very important in view of why they so desperately defended their positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And if -- assuming all of that is true, how would that operate to absolve the accused of any of the charges? This is what I'm keen to find out, how it impacts on the question of guilt or innocence, which is all that we are concerned with here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we're, first of all dealing here with an armed conflict that lasted permanently and at this stage that we are discussing, there was fierce conflict that these units were participating in, and due to that, the defence of the VRS became more persistent in order to prevent this what was threatening them from happening. If they lost their positions and if their troops fell into the hands of these detachments, it gave them additional impetus and motivation to act permanently in those days an and defend their positions in order to avoid the situation in which every prisoner, as is written here in this document, being executed the moment he is captured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, would any of this provide, in your understanding of the law, a defence in respect of the charges against the accused? I understand you to be saying that the Serbs were fearful of being captured by these foreigners and the ABiH and, therefore, they had to fight strenuously to prevent being captured. But you haven't gone further to say how, if that is so, that impacts on the guilt or the innocence or just more generally the liability of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, what the Defence is trying to do here, to prove here, that has to do with the time when General Dragomir Milosevic was commander, is that at that time, especially at the time of this offensive, the intensity or the fighting was such that they had to take all measures to save their lives and houses, primarily if they knew within that moment within the units that were operating then there were these numerous units consisting of foreign participants that could additionally endanger lives if the positions were to fall. Everything that happened during this period had to do with intensive offensive fighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think you are coming closer to linking it now. You say that the intensity of the fighting was that they had to take all measures to save their lives and houses, which, as I understand it, is something akin to saying that they had to defend themselves. Ms. Edgerton, any views on --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, precisely. Precisely. They had to defend themselves from things like that as well, and only within the Geneva Convention, to respond with adequate fire and thereby do what has to be done. In this period, only along those lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, can you just clarify this, because I think this is crucial to the case. My question is: Does the fact that the Serb soldiers would have to defend themselves so fiercely from being taken prisoners by these foreigners, would that constitute a legitimate reason to violate the laws of the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Harhoff, that is the right question. I haven't fully explained this yet. I don't think that there were any violations of laws of war at that point in time, when in those days you had against you a much better armed enemy and much more numerous enemy, including units that had such categorically principles guiding them. That is the only reason why I'm trying to explain this document. So in that situation, when you had against you an enemy which in terms of weapons and in terms of personnel levels was so much stronger, the only reason to act was to fully defend oneself and fully observe conventions of international law. This is a good example of that. And additional example of that, because within these units that were attacking the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, there was this unit consisting of 300 foreign internationals which is a large number, as it says in this document, and their guiding principle was there is no concept of a prisoner of war. That's what the document says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But, Mr. Tapuskovic, if no violations of the laws of the war were committed by members of the VRS, then how is this whole discussion relevant to the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, quite simply, how could it not be relevant to the case, if it only reinforces one's wish to defend oneself? I think that that is clear enough. And these were units that were within the units that were carrying out the offensive at that point in time, within the 3rd and 7th Corps. As Mr. Karavelic said, the 3rd and the 7th Corps was among the units that were attacking the zone that was under the control of the army of Republika Srpska. He already confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting is going to respond, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am not sure I have captured exactly what Mr. Tapuskovic has said. The way I understand it is it's -- and I think Judge Harhoff sort of got -- was getting to this point. If there are no violations of war, then it is irrelevant, because you don't need to go there. You just need a justification if no crime has occurred. If there are violations of war, then we're getting into the area of either self-defence, which I don't really understand Mr. Tapuskovic to be saying, because I don't think it's linked closely enough. I don't think it is imminent enough that it is a matter of self defence. What I think what I understand him to be saying is that it is a matter of reprisal, since it's the defence of reprisal, which is a kind of form of tu quoque. And I think it's quite clear under the law of the Tribunal that reprisals against civilian targets is not allowed under international law, and so I don't think that this is a valid Defence. So I -- it seems to me that it's either irrelevant if the defence is that there were no violations of the laws of war, or it's an invalid justification for the violations of the laws of war; and in either event, it doesn't seem to advance the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, after all of this, I have to add the following. This has nothing to do with tu quoque. There is no dispute, and we've heard from that ample evidence here, that on both sides there were a great many casualties because of this intensive permanent activity on both side. At this moment, I don't want to go into which side inflicted more casualties on the other. But at that point of intensive fighting, there were casualties on both sides. I assume that is not in dispute, in view of everything that we have heard so far. So from that point of view, in order to protect themselves from even greater casualties on their own side, they had to step up resistance, and the number of casualties stemming from the intensive fight is evident on both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, as to whether the defence that you are seeking to make out would hold up in law is another matter, and that is not for to us decide. At this stage, I'm satisfied that you have established the relevance of the line of cross-examination that you are following. Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to dwell on this document any further, but the English, page 3, last paragraph, and in B/C/S, it is the fourth page from the back, why I asked all of this so there is no repetition. "While combat activities were taking place, the foreigners from the detachment have displayed fanaticism that is based on religious fanaticism. The notion of a prisoner of war is unheard of as far they are concerned. War booty is only used for the purposes of the unit itself." This document is addressed to you by your security service, and it was signed by Colonel Cudic, assistant commander. Did you get this document?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that I don't remember, but I have heard of this document, later, though. Because this document was referred to in the Hadzihasanovic/Kubura case, as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could this be document, since it does have a translation, be admitted into evidence. DD00-1672.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes D145.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, could you just repeat it me, because I can't see the date of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The date of the document is the 9th of June, 1995; that is to say, a few days before the offensive started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there are a number of documents that are being translated now. I expect this one to come on the 10th of April, but I translated the relevant parts through a sworn court interpreter. Those are the parts that I would like to read out to the witness. DD00-0648.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if I may, once again, I -- I respectfully that the witness be allowed to see the whole document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now, what is the whole document, Mr. Tapuskovic? How many pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Six pages with the certification. I'm just using a few sentence; namely, those that were translated into English by the sworn court interpreter and translator, and they're in e-court. The document is being translated and I will receive it on the 10th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well I'm so -- just a minute. I'm so impressed by your self-help that I think we should proceed, since you went to the trouble of having a sworn court reporter translate the relevant passages. So we will proceed and in the end I will make a decision as to the admissibility of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have a hard copy in the witness' own language of the document. It has some highlighting on and my note. But since my note is in English, I don't think the witness would be able to understand it in any case. And it might assist the witness in answering the question, if he is able to have the whole document in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you have a copy in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it in e-court. The whole document is in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let us proceed, and we'll see whether the witness can say whether is he disadvantaged by not having the document in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this document was signed by Mr. Karavelic personally, the 21st of November, 1994. Later on you can take a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Before that, I would like to ask you something. You know that -- that there different kinds of rifle grenades with instant effect -- well, actually, did you say yes?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What is the range of one type and what is the range of the other type; that is, what is ejected from the shoulder, or rather, you shoot from the shoulder, as far as I know as a layman?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, and the range is, say, from 100 to 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at the beginning, the first paragraph, where you talk about the aggressor. Where you talk about the aggressor, towards the end. In English, it is page 1 of this translation of mine. Towards the end down here, you say: "In the region of the technical school museum, the aggressor acted with the grenade launcher upon the tram when the only tram driver was wounded. The 21st of November, 1994." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Towards the end, "aggressor," and then further down.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is "Operative Group 2."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I'm reading out what I think is interesting, towards the end of the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: First paragraph. "In the region of the technical school museum, the aggressor acted with grenade launcher upon the tram when only tram driver was wounded.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see something else written here. Has this been changed in my version? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No. But look at it, towards the end. "In the region of the technical school," do you see it now?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Just a moment, please. Yes. Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It is correct that 200 metres is the maximum range of that type of grenade?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, I mean, an approximation is taken because it oscillates.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, right. 200 metres, because the tram is not more than 200 metres away from the Miljacka river.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, well. You put that well, didn't you? I don't want to ask you about it any further, but this place where the tram was hit, according to the statements made by several witnesses, is at least 500 metres away from the Miljacka.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rifle grenades can be launched from different make-shift devices, as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on page 3 in the B/C/S; and in the English version, it is page 2, the first paragraph. You see 2.1?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That is not the paragraph I want, the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "In the operation zone OG 1, in the afternoon during the changing, aggressor forces active in the region of Privadol, BVG 1S, MTBR with 34 granites, MB 83 millimetre --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's Note: And 19 shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- from MB 60 millimetres very precisely, but we do not any data on aggressor's losses. With two MB 120 millimetres, one MAD proskok [phoen] and ostojice [phoen] were shooting." Is this correct? Is that what is stated in this report that you signed?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And, finally, in English it's page 2, paragraph 3 and page 4, paragraph 1, UNPROFOR activities. Please look at page 5 of the B/C/S. It says: "It was noticeable that you units of UNPROFOR were given increased measures of combat readiness. There were no special activities during the date. Today UNPROFOR did not allow the transfer of a Howitzer from Dugo Polje. It will be transferred in parts during the following day. "UNPROFOR is intensively working on the road towards Kostraca in the area of Podlugovo, a protest was launched, and the response was that they would deploy aircraft if their work is jeopardised by our unit." Is that correct, and is that your signature on the document?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand this last bit about UNPROFOR. "UNPROFOR intensively working on the record towards Kostraca, zone of responsibility OG 3, in the area of Podlugovo, probably in the area of Podlugovo; whereby, a protest was launched -- lodged, and the response was that they would deploy aircraft if our units would jeopardise their work." Who would deploy aircraft?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: UNPROFOR, NATO.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whose aircraft? Aircraft for support?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please. It is clearly written here what it was that you wrote. First of all, that you were forbidden to transfer a Howitzer, and then you take it apart and take it --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down. The interpreter did not hear the question -- the answer because the question was still going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're being asked to slow down by the interpreters; don't overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So this is correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But it is not in the transcript what you said, your answer to my question, and even my question is not in the record. That means that I will have to repeat it. It was noticeable that UNPROFOR units were given increased measures of combat readiness. UNPROFOR today did not allow the transfer of a Howitzer from Dugo Polje; and, therefore, during the course of the following day, it will be transferred in parts, in separate parts. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me whether that was correct. Well, this was prepared by officers. I just signed it. Now, is it correct? Is it correct? Probably, it is correct. UNPROFOR did not let me take a Howitzer down the road that goes through the demilitarised zone, then my centres probably decided that they would disassemble it and have it carried on horseback and go around the demilitarised zone and bring the Howitzer in separate parts on horseback. That is probably it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could this document DD00-0648 please be marked for identification, pending the translation that I will receive shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we'll mark that for identification as D146.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I have document DD00-1885. It's been translated by the CLSS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karavelic, this letter is addressed, Major-General Gobillard. The sector commander is sending this letter to you on the 4th of November, 1994, and it reads as follows: "Dear General: On the 3rd of November 1994, during an escort scheduled to pick up the Bosnian Prime Minister, Mr. Silajdzic, a convoy composed of four vehicles, two VBL and two APCs, came under fire in the vicinity of Krupac," and then we have the coordinates of this location. "As the shootings were coming from the top of the quarry, it is clear that the origin of the two firings was from the area under the control of the BH army. After the investigation, see the photos enclosed, eight impacts were detected on different vehicles. This deliberate action is unacceptable, and I would remind that we were accomplishing this mission to the benefit of your prime minister. Regards, General Gobillard." My question is: Is it possible that you were prepared to each shoot even at your own prime minister?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have document DD00-1885 be admitted into evidence as Defence exhibit because we have the translation thereof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes D147.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document is DD00-1459, which has also been translated by the CLSS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It read as follows. This is the document dated the 14th of October 1994, and here again this document was signed by Cudic, and it read as follows: "Yesterday, on the 14th of October 1994," and this is addressed to Gobillard. "Yesterday, on the 14th of October 1994, one of our soldiers tried to defect in the area of Grbavica. Our soldiers opened fire and probably wounded him. Members of the RusBat then came in APCs into the no-man's land and pulled out our soldier to the opposite side. We demand that you immediately return our soldier to our side; otherwise, we shall publicly accuse you of cooperation with the opposite side." My question is: Everyone who tried to cross over the separation line came under your fire? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess that's the fundamental and basic mission of every army engaged in a war with the opposite side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Even if we're talking about civilians?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't treat me like a child. I'm not a child.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have this document DD00-1459 be admitted into evidence as Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the translation, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. Based on the position that this Chamber took yesterday, I would suggest it would be more appropriate, especially given the witness' responses with respect to this document, for it to be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked for identification as D148.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, he gave an answer and he said it was ridiculous, and he said it was something normal. I don't see how he didn't answer this, and this document was translated. I don't have anything to do with identification. He said it was ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I said it was ridiculous to claim that my soldiers shot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please move on, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note the speaks are overlapping again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Move on and do not overlap. There's another request from the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, document DD00-1809 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskvoci, It is time for us to take the next break --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I will end with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are at the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're at the time for the break. And when we resume, I'll just spend two minutes before the witness comes into court to deal with two administrative matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The first matter relates to a confidential second motion filed on the 16th of March, 2007 by the Prosecution for the testimony of Dr. Beslic to be heard via video link conference. Now the Defence response is expected on the 30th of March, 2007. Originally this witness was expected to testify on the 2nd of April, but it is now the intention of the Prosecution to schedule him to testify between the 3rd and the 5th of April, the same dates as seven other witnesses who will also be testifying by video-conference link. In light of the need to make arrangements for the witness' testimony if he can not testify via videolink, the Prosecutor may wish to revert to the original plan of the 2nd of April. But in that event it would be helpful if we could decide this motion before the week of the scheduled videolinks. That is before Monday, the 2nd of April, and for that reason we would need to know whether the Defence response would be provided earlier than is required by the rules. Ideally then, I would think sometime this week. So I am to ask Mr. Tapuskovic whether the Defence would be in a position to provide their response. Oh, yes, I've just been reminded that tomorrow would be our last day, because we are not sitting Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my colleague can give you an answer immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Now, regarding the testimony of Dr. Beslic, Defence is not against a video-conference -- a videolink being established for his testimony and so we're -- we are giving you the answer today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes. Now the next matter is that on Monday, the 2nd, we are scheduled to hear Captain Hansen. But I note that the Prosecution only has Captain Hansen scheduled to testify. The Prosecution therefore needs to have additional witnesses because we have scheduled, I think, probably at the most, one session for Captain Hansen's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had hoped to squeeze in another witness in the extra time on Monday, the 2nd ever April, but we also did not want that witness to go into Tuesday, because the videolink is very compressed. We have eight witnesses in three days by videolink. And so we cannot go into Tuesday. We had two possibilities of witnesses to bring on the Monday, the 2nd, that we thought that the only two that we thought could fit into that little gap, neither one is able to come. One of them, in fact was Dr. Beslic and the other witness that we thought could fit into the -- that gap is simply unable to come on that date. So, unfortunately, we are going to be left with a gap on that Monday. And I apologise for that. It will have been the first time that has happened in this trial, and as I said t is necessary because we have got to start the videolink on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can Dr. Beslic be videolinked on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, setting up the videolink is a lot -- there's a lot of people involved and a lot of technology and we have scheduled it for Tuesday, and I don't know if it would be possible -- it's perhaps possible for it to be -- that we could start it on Monday and I can look into that. I'll send some e-mails right away and see if it's possible that we could actually start it on Monday and perhaps start either with Dr. Beslic or one of the other videolink witnesses and get the ball rolling. That is -- that is a good suggestion. Although I'm not sure it is possible, given all the people that have to come together to make the videolink happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think it would a feasible solution because also to have eight videolinks in one day is -- or in two days, is a bit much. So if we could start the videolink process Monday, then that means that we could have Captain Hansen and maybe one other videolink testimony on Monday, and so that will alleviate the stress on Tuesday and Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: From our side it should be no difficulty, from the side of the OTP. It's just going to be a matter of getting all the personnel there. But, I think they will be there anyhow, so by then so -- I'm optimistic that we can do that and I'm grateful for the session. Before I sit down, I have another matter to raise regarding scheduling which I can raise now or if there are other things that the Court wants to take up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No I have concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It has to do with scheduling today and tomorrow. As Your Honours know this witness was scheduled for four hours of cross-examination and there was 45 minutes yesterday and if today -- if all of today is used up that would be four hours and 45 minutes -- or four hours and 50 minutes of cross-examination. The -- my concern is about the witness tomorrow, the expert witness. He must finish tomorrow, because he -- he is in the Dutch military and is being re-deployed after his testimony tomorrow and he was brought from a location far away. He -- he is scheduled to testify one and a half hours on direct and two and a half hours on cross-examination. We will shorten or direct to one hour, in order to assist in having him complete tomorrow. Also, in the event that the Defence is unable to finish the cross-examination today and Your Honours are inclined to grant more time, I would note that we could sit extra time tomorrow. There courtroom space available. I know that I'm not sure that Judge Mindua would be available and that might be an impediment, but there is courtroom space available. I'm just making any suggestion possible so that we can finish the witness tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see absolutely no reason why this cross-examination should go beyond four hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If it finishes today, if this witness finishes today, we will have no difficulty finishing the witness tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Because we can start with the examination-in-chief of the next witness today?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No. We had actually planned to start him tomorrow at 2.15 and take an hour, and then that would leave well over two and a half hours for the Defence to do their cross-examination, actually that would leave three hours. We anticipated -- because we got an indication that he needed the rest of the day, we anticipated starting the next witness tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tapuskovic has made no such application to me. I expect Mr. Tapuskovic to utilise the time that has been allocated. The Prosecutor used two hours and seven minutes, and normally Mr. Tapuskovic would have the same amount of time. So far he has used an hour and 38 minutes. I will, of course, hear any application for an extension, but it certainly will not be going beyond the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I would just note, Your Honour, that since this was a 92 ter witness, according to the schedule from Your Honours, we were granted two hours, which we basically adhered to, and Defence was granted four hours for cross-examination. But even if they used four hours, that would be completed by the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic, please bear that in mind. And let the witness be brought in, so that we can move ahead quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may say something, please. Tomorrow's witness is not so much interesting for the Defence. I will probably cut my time allotted in half. However, this witness of today is the only military officer, the only commander who came to this Tribunal; and unless I question him as fairness would require, then I won't be in the position to raise any significant issues relating to the defence of the General accused. But no one should have any concerns. I will terminate my examination tomorrow the minute the gentleman in question needs to go. I kindly ask for the four hours to be granted to me. Tomorrow's witness can rest assured that I can release him after half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will just move from one document to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, the document DD00-1809 was signed by you. I only translated portions of it via a sworn in court translator.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So can we please have the document, DD00-1809, be -- have displayed. It's dated the 6th of April, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in one sentence only from the portion entitled,"Our forces." Towards the end of the first paragraph, you say as follows: "In the evening by action from infantry weapons prevented the attempt of defection of one person to Grbavica." It's a document signed by you. The question is: Does this imply that this person was killed and thereby prevented from crossing over?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was caught by the shoulder and pushed back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But this is what it reads in the evening, by action from PN, not that he was tapped on the shoulder and told to go back, but he had been fired on and thereby he was prevented from crossing over. He was killed?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It says here a person; it doesn't say a soldier. So I put to you that it was a civilian who was killed from infantry weapons. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have DD00-1809 be tendered for identification. I provided a translation of this one sentence only, and the signature is that of Karavelic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In -- just in advance of a submission with respect to the document, perhaps Mr. Tapuskovic could direct us to exactly where in the B/C/S original it says that somebody was killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, can you do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't understand the objection. I put a direct question to the witness and said that this person was prevented from crossing over by fire from infantry weapons, to which he said that he would just pulled by the shoulder and returned back. I was only saying to the witness that this person was killed from this kind of weapons and thereby prevented from crossing over, which he denies as being untrue. This is his document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I say that it is not true that he was just tapped on the shoulder and returned, but rather shot dead.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see it written like that anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Read the third sentences: "In the evening, by action from our forces," et cetera, read it for yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And what is the relevance of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, every man who tried to cross over was immediately executed by firing at this person. This is describes one incident only, and this is a document produced and signed by Mr. Karavelic. This document shows that by firing from infantry weapon, a person was prevented from crossing over to the other side. This is what it literally says. I don't understand how this is irrelevant. On the contrary, this is very much relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How is it relevant to the guilt or innocence of the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No one was allowed to cross over and remain alive, Your Honours. I can't believe that a question can be raised about the relevance. Every person in town who tried to get out, according to this, was immediately executed by being fired on. Not a single Serb --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry. Explain the relevance again for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Between 40 and 50.000 Serbs were in Sarajevo, and they couldn't leave Sarajevo. Whoever tried to get out and get across the separation line met the destiny described in this order issued by General Karavelic. If had is irrelevant then --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. It's not for to you. The Chamber is deliberating on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, and this was always portrayed as a consequence of sniping carried out by the Serbs. Always as a rule, a person was shot dead --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where is the evidence of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, all the civilians who got killed in Sarajevo were in huge numbers registered as victims of sniping. This is an indisputable proof that everyone to tried to cross the separation line was subjected to fire and, thereafter, it was depicted as a result of action by the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The last part is interesting, that, thereafter, it was depicted as action by the Serb. But where is that? Are you bringing evidence of that? Have we had evidence of that so far in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A few moments ago, and as a matter of fact, this document is not reflected in the transcript, I mentioned DD00-1459, which shows that -- well, this document has a translation, too; and not only a translation, but it shows that a person was fired at that had been taken over by the UNPROFOR battalion. We don't know what happened to that person, but at any rate that person had been hit. And this document was not even admitted. 1459 is the document. I cannot find -- I beg your pardon. It wasn't even marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think it was, D148.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, please, these are two documents. I cannot find many such documents but here are two of them. I have some other documents, too, but I don't want you to burden with all of that. But these show --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Tell me this. Let us assume now you're making your closing your argument. Let us assume that the case has ended, and you're making your submissions on this particular issue. What is your submission on it to have your client walk through the door a free man? Show me how this evidence enables to you do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assert, Your Honours, I assert that up to now not a single case of intentional firing at civilians has been proven. Out of all this evidence that was called here as instances of sniping, I categorically assert and I will prove that when the time comes for my own case that these people actually lost their lives in combat, not through intentional sniping. These two documents show that it was the other way around, that whoever tried to leave Sarajevo was liquidated in this way, as shown in the documents. And the victims were always portrayed as casualties of sniping from the Serb side. That is my closing argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So the sniping incidents with which the accused is charged, you will answer in the way that you just said? That they were victims, they were victims of fire from the ABiH side and that was --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- attributed to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were also casualties where representatives of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina fired at their own people. All other victims in this period of time that we are dealing with are victims of fighting that was permanent, especially during the time of the offensive, because most of the shelling victims were affected by the action coming from both sides. I'm not going into all of that now. However, since it is stated in general terms that all civilians who were killed in Sarajevo were killed because they were intentionally targeted, and these two documents show -- I'm simplifying things at this moment in time. I cannot deal with all of this now, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, bear in mind that the indictment charges that victim A died as a result of sniping or shelling. Victim B died as a result of sniping or shelling. These are specific charges and that is what have you to answer. I must also make it clear that in making these comments I'm not suggesting there is any burden on you. There is no burden on you at all to do anything, to disprove anything. You can remain silent. The burden remains on the Prosecution. But it is my duty as the Judge to understand your defence, and this is what I am trying to do. I'm having some difficulty understanding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour. May I just add one more thing. You see, he, General Milosevic, General Dragomir Milosevic, was primarily accused of killings. Everyone of those incidents was a specific killing. If the Prosecution proves all of that beyond a reasonable doubt, everyone of these incidents are things that the Defence has to deal with specifically; and when the time comes, we are going to present our own arguments stating why this was not intentional killing in any one of the case.
