I don't have to explain it now. It is not my duty to do it now, and that is not what you are asking me to do. However, these two documents show how people got killed at the separation line. From the Serb side, nobody was crossing over into Sarajevo, and nobody was liquidated the way these two people were, as reflected in these two documents. These two documents are very telling, in terms of these examples as to what happened when somebody tried to cross the separation lines, what happened to these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And what is the inference you would be asking us to draw from that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, Your Honours, one matter is what the indictment contains and the incidents. These incidents are given as representative of something that otherwise happened on a massive scale. All the civilian casualties that happened in Sarajevo, according to the Prosecution, are the result of intentional firing of the civilian population. This is one piece of evidence saying that it was actually the other way around. It is actually opposite to that. These are just two examples for which we found arguments for the time being; however, this was a mass phenomenon. So I think that these two documents are quite telling and quite self-explanatory. I cannot find 100 examples now in the documents that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I had trouble enough finding this, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you applying for the documents to be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a translation for the first one, and I want it to be admitted into evidence. The last digits are 1459. As for the other one, I have a translation and I don't understand why this would not be admitted into evidence as well, because the translation is there, just of that part. If somebody needs to have it translated in its entirety, then they can do it. But these two documents really deserve to be admitted as Defence exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Have these documents been admitted? I'll ask the court deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I show the document ID DD00-1459 was marked for identification as DD00-148 or D148. Additionally, the second document used by Defence, document ID DD00-1809, is not yet been tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll admit both.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours. May I just make one note or raise an issue with respect to DD 180 -- DD00-1809. My friend has asserted several times that is that document of General Karavelic's, and I wonder if I could suggest that the last page, which would normally bear the signature block, be shown to General Karavelic so he can, in fact, see whether or not this is his document. And, secondly, Your Honours, again, in his submissions, his latest submissions on the document, page 46, lines 23, Mr. Tapuskovic said nobody was liquidated as these two people were. Now, if that's his submission, I would ask again that he refer to -- refer us to the evidence in the original version of this document, as to the liquidation of that individual, or perhaps correct his statement on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, show the document, the last page of the document so that the witness can see the signature. And that's your document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says "General Vahid Karavelic," but it was signed by a different individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And why would that have been?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because at the time I was not in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So that's a procedure with which you are familiar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: May we ask who signed the document, and was that done after delegation from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a type of regular procedure in the chain of command. It was signed by the Chief of Staff, Brigade General Nedzad Inerdic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's move on. We have admitted both. Would you give them a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. DD00-1459, previously marked for identification as D148, will become Exhibit D148. Document ID DD00-1809 will become Exhibit D149.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to explain something to the Trial Chamber, if you allow me to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. What is that you wish to explain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, indeed. Mr. Tapuskovic is trying to launch a monstrous fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't want to hear that. Let's move on with the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Document D64 MFI DD00-0723. I now have a CLSS translation of it. This is a document from the 19th of September, 1995, which included an order signed by Fikret Prevljak, in which it says, "On the basis of the order of the 1st Corps commander and pursuant to specific information and data of UNPROFOR in the area of the city of Sarajevo, sniper fire from our units is intense. Regarding this the attention of the President of the Presidency was drawn to this and a protest was sent asking him for immediate cessation of these attacks. "In view of the warnings received from UNPROFOR and orders from the President of the Presidency, I hereby order: Immediately stop firing all types of weapons, particularly sniper rifles." Mr. Karavelic, did you order this, what is stated here, to Prevljak, to have things done as stated here.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of constant complaints, or, rather, I beg your pardon. Due to constant firing from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps at the city and the civilian population and enormous casualties sustained in the city and because of the all the protests, the many protests we sent to UNPROFOR to stop the suffering of the civilian population in town, the other side, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, asked for agreements to be reached saying that this was allegedly done by both sides when they were discussing this with UNPROFOR, that is. UNPROFOR forces never went to either side, generally trying to remain neutral. It was always easier for them to ask for the teams to get together. So, among other, I had to go and attend a few meetings. I think I even had one meeting with the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, General Milosevic, if I remember correctly. Purportedly we were supposed to stop the sniping but this was an attempt made by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps to conceal what it was that they were doing. Of course, I had to do that in order to lessen the suffering of the civilian population. So when such a complaint comes to the President of the Presidency from UNPROFOR, the President absolutely has no idea about any of this. He sends it further down though the chief of staff to me. I, as corps commander, don't know anything about this either this because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Heard enough. What is the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The next question, Mr. Karavelic, please look at the date, the 19th of September, 1995, the time of the most intensive NATO bombings. I claim, and that's why I'm asking you this, that you took advantage of September, October and November to fire incessantly at the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps because isn't it correct, you were doing then everything that NATO was doing and that you took advantage of the situation?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Your Honours. As for this date mentioned by Mr. Tapuskovic the 19th of September, 1995 I was not the commander of the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Who was, because there was done on the order of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, Please tell the Chamber what is the relevance of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in November, or, rather in September, October, and November there was no sniping at all from the side of the VRS, vis-a-vis Sarajevo, because NATO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were acting in concert and an order is issued here to stop sniper activity against the positions of the army of Republika Srpska because this NATO bomb was under way as well. The date is 19th of September, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So what? Please relate it to the issue of liability. That's what you must do. We're not carrying out an investigation into -- generally into what happened between 1993 and 1995. We have an indictment. How is it relevant to the question of whether the accused is guilt or innocent?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours, in November or in September, October and November, there was no firing at the positions of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially not in respect of Sarajevo. Absolutely none whatsoever because NATO bombing was on and the representatives of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were sniping at the positions of the army of Republika Srpska, absolutely. In September, October, and November there was no activity. And he is accused -- or, rather, indicted for that period of time as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So let us look at the indictment. Do you have the indictment? Show me the incidents in the indictment to which this would relate and how this would impact on the guilt or innocence of the accused, how it relates to the charges. You were speaking of September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are talking about September, October, and November. Count 1 of the indictment, terror, and there is an insistence of terror pursued by VRS, however in September, October and November there was no shooting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Start again. Show me the incident to which this relates.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's start from count 1 crime of terror. From on or about 10th August, 1994, that's count 1, crime of terror. That's the first count of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Stop there. Count one, crime of terror. And show me how -- show me how the -- the document which is on the screen addresses this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look at the date. It's the 19th of September. I didn't read the whole document but the date is the 19th of the September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 19th of September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But you're starting with the 8th of October, 1994. In the first schedule to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm talking about September, when NATO bombing started, as well as about October and November. At the time there couldn't have been any terror carried out by the VRS, nor the other way -- or it was actually the other way around they were the only targets of NATO and of the BH army who took the advantage of the situation. So I have to go by stages. In these last three months there couldn't possibly be any activities carried out against Sarajevo. They were just trying to save their bare lives. However, he is being charged with this period as well. That is why I presented this document to you, although I have some other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So, in fact your defence really is that the perpetrators of the violence that led to the death or injury of all these victims was in fact the -- the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in September, October and November, there were no incidents of which the accused has been accused. In there were no operations pursued by the VRS against Sarajevo, and it is absolutely true there were no activities, maybe some desperate attempts at defence but in these three months there is was not even self-defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, can I just ask you: Are you saying that the indictment should be temporary limited so as to exclude the last three months of September, October, November 1995 from the -- is that what are you aiming at?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that in my view and when the time comes for you to render your decision, I think that these three months should be removed and not dealt with at all, because if you look at the indictment there were no incidents taking place in that period, so there can be no mention or talk of any terror in these three months. I'm going to pursue this argument for other periods as well, but this is completely out of the question when we're talking about these three months. I'm talking about terror and about all other things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, of course, I'm checking the indictment. The last incident mentioned in the indictment, which mentions terror and shelling, stops on the 28th of August, 1995. Is that right? Is that what you have? Have you checked that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We're talking about Markale 2. That's Markale 2, and this was followed by NATO bombing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The accused, of course, is accountable for the period that runs from the 10th of August, 1994 until the 21st of November, 1995. If I have understood you correctly, you are saying that as far as terror and shelling is concerned, we should exclude the period that starts on the 29th of August, 1995 because the last incident takes place on the 29th of August, 1995. Have you understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can also see in the indictment that thereafter there was no shelling or sniping on Sarajevo. There were only sniping incidents committed by the BH army. There was not a single sniping incident that Dragomir Milosevic was accused after the 28th, and there was not a single shell fired and attributable to him after the 28th of August, 1995. This document that I show you talks about the sniping committed by the BH army and using it precisely to target the permanently bombed area held by the SRK. And there was not a single incident of shelling or sniping committed by the VRS that the General has been accused of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please remind me of or explain to me what connection there is between all of this and the order we have before us dated 19th of September, 1995. What is the relevance with which -- with what you put forward now, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, precisely this sniping activity is the best proof that in that period NATO and BH army acted in concert. Is only one of the examples. Sniping activity targeted civilians on the side of the VRS, and this is not the only order. There are others as well. I took one as a -- as the most striking example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What if NATO and the BH army acted in concert? Suppose that is substantiated, what are the consequences for the liability of the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like you to notice precisely this that is clearly reflected by this -- in this document. You have to weigh these things in the overall context. The allegation is that terror persisted through the whole period. This is a reverse situation. It shows that the Serbian population was subject to the terror exclusively and thereby any accusation of Dragomir Milosevic is eradicated in this particular period of time. But given the incidents cited in the indictment and the sniping that were pursued on a permanent basis that the Presidency was prompted to issue and order for them to stop is more than evident, and this clears Dragomir Milosevic of any responsibility for this period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm going to look at what you just said. It says that it shows that the Serbian population was subjected to the terror and thereby any accusation of Dragomir Milosevic is eradicated in this particular period of time. Wrong reasoning. It doesn't follow. It doesn't follow. Even if the Serbian population was subject to terror, that, by itself, that, in and of itself, does not necessarily, to use your word, "eradicate" any accusation in relation to Dragomir Milosevic. You would have to go further and to show how the terror inflicted by the Serbs impacted on the incidents set out in the indictment, whether by way of self-defence or by way of some other legitimate defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have to separate two things. It is not up to me to talk about the period, and the time will come for that, between 10th of August, 1994 and 28th of August, 1995. For that period, I have to produce for you much stronger arguments and evidence. I'm talking to you about the period during the NATO bombing. In the indictment pertaining to this period, there is not an incident cited that was committed by the VRS, either in terms of shelling or in sniping. There is not a single action attributable to Dragomir Milosevic carried out in the last three months. The Prosecution does not -- cannot cite any single incident from that period of time involving the VRS, and this document is the best illustration of what I'm saying. And it shows that the Presidency had to intervene in order to put a stop to the sniping against the other side, and probably this was drawn to their attention by NATO. As I said there was not a single incident in the period after the 28th of August, 1995, not even in the indictment, and therefore we -- there is nothing to be discussed here with regard to the activities of the VRS within the framework of the indictment. As for the previous period, however, I will have to produce different arguments for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, it seems to me that we are perhaps confounding two different aspects of two different issues. One is the temporal extension of the indictment; and if I understand you correctly, you're saying that the last three months of the period for which the accused is charged with allowing terror and other crimes to be committed in Sarajevo, that this should be excluded from the indictment because no crimes were committed from the VRS in that time. That is one issue. The other issue, as far as I see it, is the incidents that have been scheduled, both sniping incidents and shelling incidents, and I guess that for those incidents there is a case for to you answer. This is why we are here. So I suggest that we separate the issue of the temporal extension of the indictment from the other issue of your client's responsibility for the incidents that are scheduled in the indictment, and let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is precisely what I'm saying, the indictment itself shows that after the 28th of August, there was not a single incident that the accused is being charged or either in terms of shelling and sniping, not a single incident. And I'm going to prove, of course, that in August he wasn't even there. He was undergoing medical treatment at the time, and it is going to be up to you to weigh that fact. But in any case the indictment doesn't show a single incident in September, October, and November. As a matter of principle, I assert that the VRS, even before the 28th, did not commit a single war crime, and that particularly refers to the last three months --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Please, I have to stop you. I have understood your point of view. The Bench has clear understood your point of view. The difficulty I have is that I'm not sure that I can extract the same interpretation from this particular document that you are actually trying to -- to extract. But I again, I repeat, I think we should separate the two issues of the temporal extension from the scheduled incidents, and let's move back to the line of defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, proceed, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not even going to tender this. I take into account your objections. Now we have document 65 ter 01989, and until now, it was D65, MFI. And now I have a translation. It was signed by Mr. Karavelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Karavelic, this is a letter that you are writing to minister, Dr. Hasan Muratovic. "Dear Minister: In relation to" such-and-such "letter, I wish to inform you of the following. In the building of the executive council, there are no units of the 1st Corps or sniper shooters."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, do we have the translation of this letter, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Yes. There is an official translation, a CLSS translation. Now, I don't know. I have the translation. Now, whether it is in e-court or not --.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you were writing to Hasan Muratovic, and you say: "In the building of the executive council, there are no units of the 1st Corps or sniper shooters from our units." That is the 27th of August 1994. It is the MUP that is securing the building of the executive crowns with their own units. "As for this incident, General Soubirou informed Mr. Enes Bezdrob as well, and we believe that such incidents will be avoided in the future." You signed that on the 27th of August, 1994?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This was sniper shooting, which, in your assessment, was carried out by someone from the MUP. Somebody from the MUP was firing at the civilians?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, there wasn't any sniping there at all, so what is this all about? Had I received such a document from Minister Muratovic, where he asked me about this, and then he was probably informed according to the same system as the one that I explain add while ago. And I'm telling him that I do not have any units of my own within, and that that the building is under the authority of the MUP. And it was usually one or two policemen that were providing security for the building. They stood in front of the entrance in most cases, because the building could also be used from the basement side, and it could be accessed that way and the basement was even used for important meetings. I'm telling you again that I just had to use the word "snipers" or "sniper shooters" just because I would get that kind of term from up above. They used that term, "snipers." However, please, in order to understand this properly, snipers were in rifle squads, in the lowest structural unit, and snipers were -- were treated just like any other soldiers or riflemen in my case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You drew my attention to this in the third paragraph that such incidents should be prevented. It is my suggestion that this letter was written either because a French soldier was hit, an UNPROFOR soldier, or a civilian, and that is why the protest was made?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document please be admitted into evidence. We now have a translation as well. Until now it was just marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this was previously marked for identification as D65. It is now admitted as Exhibit D65.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Document DD00-0681 until now was D66 MFI.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In order to avoid reading all of it out to you, and there is a translation of it as well, Alija Izetbegovic wrote a letter to your superior, General Delic, and warned him that the French ambassador -- the Ambassador of France told him that military expertise showed that one of their soldiers had been hit from BH army positions. And that as a matter of fact more than half of the 24 killed soldiers were killed by the representatives of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Were you aware of this letter, and did your superior, Delic, inform you about it?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many such letters. I repeat, a great many. My response to this letter would be the following and I'll just going to read a paragraph from this letter. He stated that when the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina allows the UNPROFOR commission to enter the buildings from where the bullet could have been fired at the French soldier, it will be possible to speak of normalisation of relations between Paris and Sarajevo. My comment: In part of this letter, in says that the VRS was cooperative in investigating and touring locations in terms of the possible firing position from where the bullet came from and that my side conditionally speaking did not allow that. And you see from here, from this part where it says quite literally that one building, or, rather the most suspicious point from where the bullet was fired killing the French soldier could not have been inspected because it was forbidden by the VRS. Without any impartiality, without any partiality I wish to say that these letters are irrelevant, such letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just one question. One more. This letter was written by Alija Izetbegovic to Delic and you are saying that saying that it is irrelevant in your view?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Alija Izetbegovic doesn't know anything about fighting. The poor man, he was a person who had no idea what a rifle was and what a bullet was. He just worked on the basis of what was submitted to him by the army of Republika Srpska or, rather, UNPROFOR and then he would sent it down to us to eliminate all these doubts and suspicions and that's what we always did. I would just like to say one sentence to the Trial Chamber, if I may. I was commander of the 1st Corps. My assistant for legal affairs was a Serb and he was the most important one there, a Serb. Zlatko Petrovic was his name. My assistant commander for morale in my corps, the corps that His Honour, the Judge called them Muslim army, yesterday, he was a Serb, a Colonel Mihajlovic. In my corps I had very many officers who is were Serbs and Croats. I was not fighting for the Muslims. I was, but through my struggle for a comprehensive Bosnia-Herzegovina, multi-ethnic, and multi-cultural, multi-confessional, as opposed to other armies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you for the explanation. Next question, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, in relation to this, have I nothing else. But can this 66 MFI since it has a translation now, be admitted into evidence as a Defence exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is marked for identification as D66. It now becomes Exhibit D66.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karavelic, now I have a document that was translated by a sworn court interpreter and a translator in its entirety and you signed it. Or, rather, it says here that it is your document. I cannot see the signature here. I got it from the archive of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or, rather, from the Office of the Prosecutor, and DD00-053 is the number. And I will slowly read it out to you. This is a document dated the 30th of September, 1994, and it is called procedure towards UNPROFOR forces. The following procedure is to be taken towards UNPROFOR forces. Leading of units that enter into through the zone of exclusion of 20 kilometres in addition to UNPROFOR forces to be carried the out in total secrecy hide and mask the operation and deployment of units. Units that carry out the attack at the front line in the exclusion zone and in the UNPA as per agreement dated 13th of August, 1993? In the stage of transporting, getting under and incoming also take measures of hiding, up to arrival of units to positions. In case that UNPROFOR forces uncover the presence of our units in mentioned zones, through the contact of unit commanders or other authorised officers, an attempt should be made to solve the situation by carrying out the task. In case UNPROFOR forces try physically through use of force to prevent carrying out this task, to all their acts response reciprocally to demonstrative acts of UNPROFOR respond by demonstrative acts, to the acts of fire upon our forces, people and technical equipment, respond by fire in order to protect the lives of our fighters and carrying out of task. Please, is that what was done in actual fact and was that document that you signed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before that, explain the relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is D53 already admitted through a previous witness. And it shows that the exclusion zone was affected or violated and that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was always prepared. If they were stopped from affecting the exclusion zone, they would always fire at UNPROFOR initiatives. That is what the document says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The question is: Was that actually done in actual fact? Did you camouflage your equipment and your movements? Did you violate the exclusion zone and even fire at UNPROFOR units?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order for things to be clear to the Trial Chamber, the demilitarised zone at Igman was established after a big offensive launched by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps from the direction of Trnovo via Igman towards Hadzic. The objective was for Sarajevo to be placed in the second ring. That was in June and July, 1993. When we stopped at the very last moment, there were two kilometres left for this to be joined up; and when the international community reacted, the explicit request of the army of Republika Srpska was to create this demilitarised zone that I cannot show you here now, but it would be a very good thing for me to show it to you. It -- its shape was that of a curve --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could this be a bit shorter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In relation to this, I would propose another exhibit signed by Karavelic on the 12th of November, 1994, number DD00-1734. And I have a full translation provided by a sworn in-court interpreter so that the Trial Chamber can follow the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I think you said that the former document was -- had been admitted as D53. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: D53 is a statement by Fraser, and this doesn't look to me as something that Fraser could have been involved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was admitted into evidence through Witness W-46. We may check the number. If it wasn't admitted, then I have to make a proposal in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That is exactly why I'm raising the point. Perhaps the court deputy could confirm whether D53 was the document that we have just seen.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. That is the document that we just saw as the order by Karavelic, and it was admitted on the 8th of February through David Fraser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karavelic, you can see this document, dated the 12th of November, taking measures in the zone of exclusion around Sarajevo. I'm not going to read all of it. Let's just focus on paragraph number 1. "On several occasions we have been assured..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Counsel is not reading paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "... acquired information that UNPROFOR has available precise data on the stated activities and locations of weapons of the army of the Republic BH in the zone of exclusion. This data UNPROFOR gathers by using the most sophisticated radar and other reconnaissance means, and the same are very effectively used for the purpose of damaging the reputation of the army of the Republic BH before the international community.". And now this is followed by your order: "Take immediately measures to full application of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Camouflaged discipline in the region locations of disposition of weapons, calibre over 12.7 millimetre that is being situated in the zone of exclusion, radius 20 kilometres around Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My question is: You had heavy weapons all the time in the -- within the exclusion zone of heavy weaponry? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you don't -- do not deny this being your document and signed by you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the stamp with my signature, but in any case it's my document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since I have full translation if someone wants to challenge it. I would nevertheless like to have this entered as Defence exhibit, and its number is 001734.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And its importance is the suggestion that you're making that they had heavy weapons within the exclusion zone. Is that the significance of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And constantly firing from them, as I'm going to demonstrate through the following documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. The witness did answer that no, but that is your position. You're asking for us to admit it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes D150.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like now to raise a very important topic, and I have document DD00-1819 in that regard. This document is in e-court; however, its B/C/S version was a little bit blurred. In the meantime, I did manage to find a more legible copy, and I would like it to be put on ELMO for the witness, because in e-court it is not precisely legible. And I also have a translation provided by a sworn in-court interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It's a document sent to all corps commands on the 17th of August, 1995. And if you look at it, this is what it reads: "In the last 15 to 20 days, an American peace initiative has appeared for Bosnia." And it says that "President Clinton is in his fourth year of term and that the unsolved question of BH is still hanging as a democracis [as interpreted] sort. Due do that, he decided to take peace initiatives from the hands of Europe and deal with it on his own. He will try to stop the war at any cost. "Due to potentially unfavorable development of the peace initiative for BH and with the view to creating favourable conditions for negotiations by the government, I hereby order to intensify active combat operations in battlefields, but well prepared and with favourable results. On page 2, you can see that this was signed by Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at item number 4 in both versions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "A peace initiative envisages potential cessation of combat which is an additional reason for achieving favourable results in the battlefield." Do you know that on the 17th of August, Rasim Delic issued this order? He was the Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about it personally, because in that time precisely, which is the first half of August 1995, I was dismissed from my post of the corps commander. But I don't see any -- any special about this. It's very normal, because at the negotiating table it was very important who had advantage on the battlefield. And this was imposed by the VRS, and the international community accepted that. It just stamped and approved the results achieved in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to try to finalise before the break, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: To finalise your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I guess that would be hoping too much. Just to finalise this question. All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So the order was to intensify the fighting and that is what happened?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened hundreds of times in war. I don't know about there particular one, but it is very possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have this document admitted as exhibit, DD00-1819, along with the translation provided by a sworn in court translator.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that becomes D151.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic, and you must endeavour to conclude your cross-examination within the time remaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is absolutely impossible, Your Honours. This is out of the question. I have so many important documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I worked with Judge May, and in these circumstances he would say, Let's see how we get on. So let's see how we get on. He's a good man to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. I will do my best to be as efficient as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karavelic, some things that are not in dispute we can deal with quickly. Document DD00-0751; that's a schedule of passage through the tunnel. You do not deny the existence of this tunnel that you used for passage?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one alive denies that, and Vahid Karavelic is the last person to deny it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If you can take a look at this document, DD00-0751, and confirm that you regulated how this tunnel is going to be used. Just look at it, and confirm that this is how it happened. And we also have an English translation provided by the CLSS. It was signed by Prevljak by your authorisation, and this stipulates the times of passage through there tunnel. This document consists of two pages?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see this is Fikret Prevljak's order, and in this he refers to my order. I guess that is what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can I please have this admitted into evidence as a Defence exhibit. This only regulates the schedule of the passage through the tunnel and who is going pass through it, and we have full translation of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honours, I have no objection to this document, and the witness has spoken about it. But I think it's to everyone's advantage if we can ask that we scroll through the document of several pages, which actually purports to attach the witness's order, so he could probably actually see his order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Let's do that. Let's show the witness the order which he himself made. Can we scroll through it? Is that the technical term? Scroll down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness explained that Prevljak issued this order on his authorisation, and this is what it says on page number 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, what is your interest? Is that to see that Prevljak passed the order on, or is it to see the order itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It reads here: "Pursuant to the order of the 1st Corps," and this is Mr. Karavelic. Prevljak regulated and designed the schedule of who is going to pass through the tunnel at 6.00 a.m., at 9.00 a.m., and 12.00, et cetera. And I believe that Mr. Karavelic can confirm this. That's the first thing. Of course, he may look at, but I think it is not a good use of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, if I may, I think there is it another question in here that hasn't been, in fact, put to the witness. When my friend said at page 72, line 2, Prevljak regulated and designed the schedule of who is going to pass through the tunnel at 6.00, at 9.00, and at 12.00. In fact, if he wants the General to confirm this, perhaps he could put that to the General and see if that's indeed the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, General, look at page 2.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not clear to me who drew up the schedule relating to the tunnel. Was it me or Prevljak?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Prevljak.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But he is referring here to my order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No. He is just saying that this was done pursuant to your order, that he drew up this schedule pursuant to your order. For the purpose of operization [as interpreted] of this facility and for the most effective and efficient use of the tunnel, he determined who and when is going to pass through the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not what is written here. In his document, he says only that he passed on my order and that is all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, did the schedule of the passage through the tunnel exist or not? Was it regulated?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was this order that pertains to it?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, what are you trying to show? Is it that the tunnel was used for the passage of troops?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And based on the existence ever this tunnel, I would like to ask the following: Can we speak at all about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. Just let me -- I'm not sure whether the Prosecution is disputing that the tunnel was used for military purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Not at all, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. So you needn't bother. They are not disputing that. They concede it was used for military purposes, for the transport of troops and weapons as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then we could have this document admitted into evidence. I would like to proceed immediately to that stage. This document indisputably speaks about the existence of the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In the future, you need not concern yourself with evidence to establish the military use of the tunnel, because the Prosecution has conceded or is conceding that it was used for military purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But I asked the witness after he conceded the existence of the tunnel. We cannot talk any longer about the siege ever Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can the witness comment on that because the units, and let me not proceed with my question.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I can. Sarajevo was under siege since April 1992 until the end of 1995 after the tunnel was built, and if I may just make an observation, which is actually a disgrace for the international community and the VRS. For me to build this tunnel and humiliate ourselves to go under ground, under the very eyes of the international community, nothing changed in the status of the siege of Sarajevo. The city of Sarajevo was still without electricity until the end of the war. It was without gas --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have a sufficient answer to the question. Let's move on. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you believe that I shouldn't be tendering this the all into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it. We admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] DD00-0751.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become D152.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] DD00-0747. Could Mr. Karavelic please have a look at it. There's a translation as well from the CLSS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 25th of April, 1995. It speaks of rotation of units, and in the first paragraph it says: "In order to carry out the regular planned rotation of units, battalions of the 12th Division, KOV, resubordinated to the 16th Division command and with a view to taking all the necessary measures to prepare an organisation units to leave for rotation." Can you see this?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is this an order regulating the exit of units from Sarajevo going to positions in order to help the 12th and 14th Divisions?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: A witness was heard here, and I don't think it was a protected witness, Hadzic, Ismet Hadzic. The 6th of March, 2007 is the date of his testimony, and the transcript pages are 3289 and 3290. This is where he said that there were 15 day shifts, that they would return to Sarajevo to get some rest, and then yet again they went out to their military positions. Did units in Sarajevo take rest so that they could be well rested when being on positions outside Sarajevo thanks to the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. The units were defending Sarajevo and holding positions in Sarajevo in order to prevent VRS from entering the city of Sarajevo, and most often I would send reserve units outside Sarajevo into combat there. Upon return, possibly some of them did get some rest, but most of them did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: However, can you tell me any movement by the military at the entrance into the tunnel and in zones that were near the exit out of the tunnel, wouldn't that be a legitimate military objective for this army that is on the move, moving out to a combat mission?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The exit and the entrance of the tunnel was always a military objective for the army of Republika Srpska. I sustained terrible casualty there at both sides of the entrance into the tunnel. There was shelling, regardless of who or what was going through the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document 04747, since it has a translation as well, be admitted into evidence as a Defence exhibit straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes D153.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I have DD00-0741, which also has a translation provided by the CLSS, dated the 1st of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You see it's the 12th Division again, and it says here, "Execution of attacks." And in the text it says: "The experience obtained so far in carrying out surprise raids both in the zone of the 1st Corps as well as in the zones of the other corps has shown that there is a need and that it is important to carry out sabotage actions in the PZT. "Between the 26th and 27th of the June, 1995, in the early morning of the 27th of June, 1995, the 2nd K corps units prepared and successfully executed a surprise attack at," and then it says where. "The aggressor suffered significant losses, 40 Chetniks were killed, more than double this number were wounded, and a wounded Chetnik was captured and taken to hospital, some 40 to 50 infantry weapons," and so on "were captured as well." "The commanders of the units every day in accordance with the -- through daily assessment of the situations and use of the units in carrying out combat operations, unit commanders shall plan in accordance with the existing conditions and carry out surprise BD in the enemy's immediate rear and deeper behind the lines." And then paragraph 4, that is the only thing I am showing here now: "By carrying out sabotage actions against PZT with the aggressor constantly cause fear, panic," and so on. This order was issued by Fikret Prevljak, commander of the 12th Division. You are aware of this order at the time of the combat actions in June 1995? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would suggest that you read paragraph 4 in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I will. "And so tie down part of their forces in securing features against which sabotage operations can be carried out successfully."

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And its objective is to prevent continued attacks against the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karavelic, this refers to the period of time of the offensive between June and late July 1995, so an offensive launched by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the 30th of June, when the offensive was stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document, DD00-0741, be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D154, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now I have a Defence Exhibit, or rather, a document DD00-0909. Until now, it was D110 MFI. This is an order dated 20th of May, 1995, within the 12th D KOV. "Bearing in mind the importance of relations in RIK units in all wartime conditions, I hereby order. All vital features, Grdonj, Borije, Colina Kapa, Debelo Brdo, Mojmilo, Azici, Stupsko Brdo, Vis, Zuc, the Faculty of Traffic and Transport Engineering must have wire communications from two sides. Chief of Staff, Colonel Rizvo Pleh. The Deadline for completion of this task is the 25th of May, 1995." Is this a fact that all these hills enumerated here were held by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and were linked up by wire communications permanently, especially in the period referred to here?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the city of Sarajevo, I had my personal wire telephone communication; and all the PTT telephone communications of Sarajevo, I used from even the last houses on the outskirts of the town of Sarajevo. And I took this line, this land line, all the way to the trenches outside the city of Sarajevo. So I had hundreds of thousands, if I can put it that way, telephone numbers on the line of siege. This saved the city of Sarajevo to a great degree. I see that what you think is that, for example, when Grdonj is mentioned, of course, it goes without saying. Because from the very last settlement on the slopes of Mount Grdonj and to the houses close to the very top of Grdonj, I dug a big dugout, a communication trench from two to two and a half metres so that people could come to these positions. That meant I that I had one-third of -- of the slope of Grdonj under my control. The rest was held by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. So also there are others, and you enumerated a great deal of these locations that can be discussed. Some can be discussed but then some others need not be discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hold the hilltops mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Grdonj, no; Borije, no; Colina Kapa, yes; Debelo Brdo, no; Mojmilo, half of it I did; Azici, half of it I did; Stupsko Brdo, half of it I did; These, I don't know which these refers to here; Zuc, yes; The Faculty of Traffic and Transport Engineering, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you hold the slope of Grdonj above Sedrenik?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The slope facing town, yes. I explained that a few moments ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could we please have a look at map 500, or rather, P500, and also the place where Grdonj is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, could the transcript reflect that I was talking about Grdonj. Sedrenik is what I referred to at the end of the sentence, because there is a question mark here. Sedrenik, in line 10. Line 10, at the end of the line, there shouldn't be a question mark but Sedrenik should be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Before I put some questions regarding this map, yesterday, you talked about some positions on the map from the Galic times, where there were some heavy weaponry. Remember that? I would like to ask you the following: The heavy weaponry, after the 10th of July, or rather, the 10th of February, when the total exclusion zone was established, these heavy weapons were no longer within a 20-kilometre diameter around Sarajevo but they were under UNPROFOR control, right?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, within a 20-kilometre diameter, but all gathered in one place, or perhaps in those places where they were under UNPROFOR control. They were not taken anywhere out of this perimeter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But from August 1994 until May, no one touched them from these positions until the end of May 1995?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, so many things happened that I cannot give you a precise answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: However, Witness Harland, who was questioned here on the 15th of January, 2007, it was said that about 317 times between the 10th of February and the 27th of April, 1994, there were 318 cease-fire violations by the BH army registered in Rose's time? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had stopped launching offensive actions from the town of Sarajevo a long time before that, simply because I did not stand a single chance of dealing with the very strong artillery of the SRK. If what the representatives of UNPROFOR said -- Well, I cannot confirm that. But if is it true, there was certainly a good reason for that because there would be an attempted infantry attack on a certain axis, where there had to be intervention so there would not be a breakthrough of the SRK force, so they would not break into the city of Sarajevo. It wasn't that I was just playing around with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, please, this document, D110 MFI, and also was marked as DD00-0909, could it please be admitted into evidence, because we have a translation and we also have the witness's answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document marked for identification as D110, now becomes Exhibit D110.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Honourable Witness, could we please now have a look at this map that is it in front of you. Yesterday, you marked some lines here that change what is on this map. Is this a combat map of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the time that this map pertained to?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general terms, in principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You never changed it before? Is only now ten years later that you put in these additional lines; is that right.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not right. I beg your pardon, but you really do not understand things. There were hundreds and thousands of maps like this that were drawn during the course of the war. Every ten or fifteen days a new map is drawn, because of changes, because of new facts, because of new data. And the existing one would be sent into the archives. Now, if I were to change everything that a low-ranking officer did, who did not know how to do things precisely as properly, that didn't really matter. It was important what was the situation on the ground, not on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You took one map out of maybe hundreds.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I have many more official maps, and this map was shown to you by the Prosecution. I do apologise for overlapping with the witness. This map was shown to you by the Prosecution not by me. Are you trying to say that the map drawn up during the event does not correspond to the factual situation, but rather what you drawn on the map?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I put in this map indicates one of the longest period that this line was here, but only in this little section here on the southern and eastern slopes of Grdonj and southern slopes of Spicasta Stijena. After consulting battalion and brigade commanders, I did that. But I myself didn't know precise line around the whole of the city of Sarajevo, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And according to these new lines that you put, if we look at the peak of Spicasta Stijena, it seems that the VRS was on the slopes rather than on the peak of Spicasta Stijena?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're talking to me, and I was there and you were not. And now you're telling me that they were on the slopes, et cetera. The plateau of Grdonj itself has a flat area. I think it was 50 by 50 metres in size, and somewhere in the middle is this trig point 906 metres. That's the elevation, 906 metres. In these houses here on the northern side, there was defence rampart of the SRK, and I was on the other side on the southern slopes. And I had vertically dug out communicating trenches towards the southern settlement, and I believe, and this is my opinion, that this is how the line should look like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I just think it would be easier for all us to see what the witness is pointing to when he talks about geographic features, Your Honour. Perhaps he can do that with the marking pen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you demonstrate what you just indicated on the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, there's a cluster of houses that can you see here. In these clusters of houses were the ramparts or defences of the SRK. I'm showing you here now the elevation point 906, and this is taken to represent the very peak of a certain feature. My line was the blue line, as I have drawn it here. Only I had, if I may also draw it, a trench that I had dug vertically. From up there downwards to the settlement and this street, I had to dig this trench more in the southwesterly direction. Because on the other side, on the south of Trebevic, where SRK had their positions, I wanted to avoid my soldiers while ascending the hill being fired upon by the SRK and where we sustained heavy casualties. Now this blue line, which goes towards east, went below Spicasta Stijena; whereas, here at the very top there was a plateau, I just said of some 50 metres in diameter. And we indeed encircled it from the south side, and from the north it was encircled by the SRK. However, Spicasta Stijena, to the east, elevation 895, on the very edge and on the very top and on the very trig point, this is where the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps forces had their positions. If I may add one thing more, both from Grdonj and particularly from Spicasta Stijena, the whole area, if I may draw a line and extend it like this, all the way like this, for example, this whole area was being observed with the naked eye extremely well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But these lines that you just now put, according to earlier enumeration, you were above this ravine. However, with these new lines, you have now put it inside the area of responsibility of the VRS. Now, when you re-drew this map, this is what the outcome seems to be?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I did initially. I said there were mistakes both in terms of the red line and the blue lines, and many mistakes simply because this map was drawn up inaccurately by incompetent officers. And I repeat again --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, if we can safe some precious time. Who was above whom? Were you at a higher elevation if you were at Grdonj with regard to Spicasta Stijena?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Always both at Grdonj and Spicasta Stijena the troops of the SRK were above us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, you assert that these new lines that you put correspond to the actual situation, and that the officers who were in charge of doing that during combat did it wrongly?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You don't have to believe me. Come and talk to hundreds of thousands of troops who were in Sarajevo. You could have done that before, you can do it now, you can do it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You did the same with Debelo Brdo. We don't have time to go back to that. You changed the former lines.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was will be best if you asked UNPROFOR about this, because it was UNPROFOR who had an observation point at the very top of Debelo Brdo for a very long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can we not remove this map from the screen, because if we remove from the screen it's not going to be retrievable again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can just as well admit it as either the exhibit for the Defence for the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but you made --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Just the Defence exhibit not -- sorry, just the Prosecution Exhibit not the Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm asking you if you're going to need this map?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. I thought so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may add --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please don't volunteer. We have counsel to ask questions, and we will also ask questions. Yes. We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be admitted as Exhibit P513.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now move to document DD00-1606. It's also been translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Honourable Witness, we have a translation of this document provided by the CLSS. Supreme Command staff is sending this letter to the 1st Corps, and it says, "According to the information available and intelligence gathered on the ground, it has been established that there is general low manpower among Chetniks," and then further on it says that "they have been plagued by panic, disorder, and fear." Can you see this?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then in the next passage, it says that they are particularly angry because they are receiving no help from their -- from Serbia; and according to their estimations, they cannot reply on them any longer. Question is: After the sanctions had been imposed by the FRY, according to the information, it should they were in a desperate situation, with no help provided either in manpower or anything else?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is -- these are rough estimates that we made. We simply thought that the army of the Republika Srpska cost the army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia so much, and that in late 1994, and indeed it was felt during 1995, that they turned off the taps, at least in comparison to how much had been provided to Pale during 1992, 1993, and 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, can we have document DD00-1696 be admitted into evidence as Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes D155.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, now I have a document that on the 19th of September, 1994 you yourself signed. I have a full translation provided of this document by a sworn in-court interpreter. No, no. Actually, I mean only the part which speaks about "Our forces." You will see after you have looked at the document. DD00-1700. We have a translation of this particular portion. It says here point 2 -- item 2 point 1, "Our forces, at Sarajevo battlefield, our forces on the day of the 18th of September, 1994 have been executing combat actions in order to occupy Spicasta Stijena and Mala Kula. For these tasks, forces were engaged comprising one platoon from 120 BBR; Crni Labudovi, platoon PTDO MUP Bosna; observation and diversion platoon of the 105th Motorised Brigade; the second -- two platoons for intervention from 105 MTBR; pioneer platoon, engineering platoon, and two company in reserve also from 105th MTBR. "Upon commencement of action, 120th Mountain Brigade have captured a part of Spicasta Stijena. The unit PTDO MUP Bosna have executed the attack right of Spicasta Stijena, and the same have, upon commencement of attack, destroyed the first trench. Further advancement was not possible due to," and then it says, "during the execution of the attack itself, the aggressor used" so-and-so "weapons," and you held this until the morning hours. My question is: Did you very often attempt to capture Spicasta Stijena? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Spicasta Stijena is the name that I think through the four years of war Sarajevo was most frequently used and uttered by a large number of people, precisely because of what was happening there and what the consequence. At one point President Izetbegovic, I think, called me directly, precisely because a huge number of complaints of citizens sent to the President claiming that it was impossible to live at the foot hill of the Spicasta Stijena. He told me, Please, can you finally do something about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Answer the question directly. Did you very often attempt to capture Spicasta Stijena?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not often. I didn't try to capture Spicasta Stijena on many occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you do know that Spicasta Stijena was the most important feature for the VRS; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, and I don't see any reason why it should have been. It was an erroneous military assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. After this hill was a road that was cut off -- had it been cut off, the VRS would have been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was out of the question. That was impossible. The VRS had so much free space that, if need be, they could have constructed a new road. It was a piece of cake for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where was that possible among those hills? You know that very well.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They circumvent a hill and build another road. That's what they did with this road. They built it during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can with he have this document, DD00-170, be tendered into evidence as a Defence exhibit, and we have a translation of this document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D156, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] DD00-1703, dated the 18th of September, 1994. Yes. There is a translation as well. This is a document issued by Rasim Delic on the 18th of September, and it speaks of combat action. In the first sentence, it says: "In the zone of the 1st Corps, combat operations are also planned, and your combat operations can commence as soon as they start." This is sent to the IBOG command, the commander personally. Do you remember that.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not going to tender it. Now I have document DD00-1708. It has also been translated where it says -- and it is also sent to all corps commanders. The first paragraph says: "In certain minor RBH army units, there are quite a few individuals who are prone to alcohol abuse and are causing incompetences. Some of the incidents were quite serious because they endangered the personal safety of the citizens and their property, the reputation of the RBH army." You know about that phenomenon, about this inappropriate behaviour of a large number of your soldiers?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the behaviour of a large number of soldiers, but rather minor infractions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just something else from this document. In paragraph 4, the 19th of September, 1994, where it says: "The RBH army has matured into a strong armed force." Was that correct already in September, that Mr. Delic concluded that at that point the 19th of September, the BH army was a mature military force? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what was he supposed to say, that we don't stand a chance of defending ourselves and that the morale of soldiers could drop below zero. He had to say something to boost morale in units in order to bolster the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, whether this has anything to do with the truth, that is it a completely different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, please, this document, DD00-1708, could it please be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How can it mature into a respectable army, when it is not manned properly, not even 10 percent--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have already given your answer. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be admitted as D157.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I have document DD00-1719. That is an order dated the 2nd of November, 1994, addressed to all corps. It has a CLSS translation, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You see this? This is an order issued by Commander Rasim Delic to all corps, and where it says, "In the preamble, it is evident that in certain units after successful breakthroughs and achieving without many losses, there follows as regular dropping and lessening of one's guard," and so on, and then the order. And then the last paragraph: "Having in view the growth of the offensive character of army operations, it is necessary to properly and consistently carry out the points of this order so that losses after successful actions are reduced to a minimum." This was sent to your corps, too. Was that the way it was, that the offensive actions of your army went up in 1994?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a general question. I tried to take the initiative. Whether I actually did, I don't know myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I didn't manage to liberate Sarajevo, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document, 1719, which has a translation, could it please be admitted into evidence as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you promised us a whole batch of very important documents. I wouldn't mind admitting this into evidence, if you insist, but I really can't see the relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the next one is supposed to corroborate this in the right way. One document has to be link the up with another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I can't wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you admit this into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become Exhibit D158.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, throughout the Autumn of 1994, these operations were on permanently. Document DD00-1728. It has a translation, too, and it says in paragraph 1: "Units and commands of the 1st Corps engaged in the Nisic battlefield encouraged by previous success in crushing the Chetniks along the axis that run from Olovo and Vares towards Srednje, crushed the Chetnik forces and liberated large areas comprising of dozens of villages; Cece, Gornja Korita, Trebina, Kostica, Pakline, Matici, Visnjica, Nisici, Ilici, Buljetovina, Hadzici, Zubeta," et cetera. And important features: Macak, Toljenak, Vrhovi, Borovo Brdo, Krst, and Kicelj. Mr. Karavelic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is this related to any of the charges, any of the incidents?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The intensity of the fighting, Your Honours, was such that this was ongoing, permanently from September 1994 and particularly in the summer of 1995, and there were casualties on both sides. To the greatest possible degree this shows how many settlements in the area of responsibility of the 1st Corps had been captured with fierce fighting and major casualties on both sides. That has to do be relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What does it have to do with the charges?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, everything that is a result of the great number of casualties sustained in this area of the 1st Corps and the army of Republika Srpska, all these casualties of the intensive fighting on both sides - at this moment, I am not going to access which side more, which side less - but this was a front line. And from one minute to the other, there were offensive or defence activities going on, and there casualties sustained by both sides and the casualties were primarily the result of this offensive action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll take the night to deliberate on this matter of the general line of questioning, and I'll give my view on it when we resume tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But let this document be admitted into evidence, DD00-1728.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have 1995 to deal with in particular, Your Honours, and that includes most of these orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I read the record correctly then, you would have just admitted the document into evidence about which the witness has not been asked a single question. I stand to be corrected, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think you're right because I stopped him before he was able to ask a question, so we'll take that up tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 29th day of March, 2007, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.02 p.m.,
